name: Hastings
summary: The East Sussex port that gave its name to the battle of 1066: home of the Haestingas and a mint town in the reign of Æthelstan, first King of the English, where William the Conqueror built his first castle in England, then the seat of a Norman lordship, a head port of the Cinque Ports, and the town nearest Battle Abbey on the battlefield inland.
overview: Hastings grew in the valley between the East and West Hills on the Sussex coast, a beach port without a sheltered harbour whose people were remembered as a distinct folk, the Haestingas, into the eleventh century. William of Normandy fortified it after landing nearby in 1066, and the battle he won some 10 kilometres inland took its name. The town became the centre of the Rape of Hastings under the Counts of Eu and a leading member of the Cinque Ports, while the abbey William founded on the battlefield grew into the town of Battle. Storms in 1287 and French raids in 1339 and 1377 ended its days as a major port.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Hastings lies on the East Sussex coast where a valley cuts through sandstone cliffs between the East Hill and the West Hill. It never had a sheltered natural harbour: its boats worked from the beach and from inlets that storms repeatedly rearranged, and the forest of the Weald behind it and the marshes of Pevensey and Romney on either side cut it off from the rest of Sussex and Kent. That isolation kept a local identity alive for centuries and made this stretch of coast an obvious landing place for anyone crossing from Normandy.

The town is famous for a battle fought elsewhere. On 14 October 1066 William of Normandy defeated Harold Godwinson on the ridge where the town of Battle now stands, and the name of Hastings, where the Norman army had its castle and camp, was attached to the battle by the time of Domesday Book in 1086. In the centuries that followed Hastings was a castle town, a Cinque Port and a fishing community, until the sea and French raiders ruined its harbour trade in the fourteenth century.

contentSections.title: The Haestingas
paragraphs: The name comes from the Haestingas, the followers of a man called Haesta, a people settled between Pevensey and the Kentish border. Symeon of Durham records that Offa of Mercia defeated the gens Hestingorum in 771, and by 790 Offa was confirming grants of land at Hastings to the abbey of Saint-Denis near Paris. Some historians think a sub-king named Watt, who witnesses the charters of the South Saxon king Nunna, ruled this people, but the idea rests on place-names alone.

The Haestingas kept a separate identity long after Sussex had been absorbed into Wessex: the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 1011 lists them beside Kent, Sussex and Surrey among the lands the Danes overran. Under the laws of Æthelstan, grandson of Alfred and first King of the English, issued around 928, Hastings was named among the towns allowed to strike coin, which shows that it was already a trading town with a market. The Chronicle's Hæstingaceaster of 1050 may mean Hastings, or, since the ending usually marks a Roman fort, the old Saxon Shore fort at Pevensey.

contentSections.title: 1066: landing, castle and battle
paragraphs: William's fleet landed at Pevensey on 28 September 1066, and within days his army moved east to Hastings and threw up a wooden castle on a mound, probably reusing an earlier earthwork. The Bayeux Tapestry shows labourers digging it under the words that William ordered a castle to be dug 'at Hestenga ceastra'. From this base the Normans raided the surrounding country, probably to provoke Harold into fighting quickly. A new settlement was already growing in the valley to the east; Domesday Book records a new borough there, which local tradition dates to 1069.

The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October about 10 kilometres to the north-west, on a ridge between Caldbec Hill and Telham Hill, and ended with Harold dead and his army destroyed. Contemporaries did not name it after the town: the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says only that the armies met at the hoary apple tree, and Orderic Vitalis, writing in the twelfth century, called the field Senlac. Domesday Book in 1086 already spoke of the battle of Hastings, naming it after the port that had been William's base.

contentSections.title: The castle and the Counts of Eu
paragraphs: After the conquest William divided Sussex into rapes, each running inland from the coast and centred on a castle, and around 1068 he gave Hastings Castle and the easternmost rape to his kinsman Robert, Count of Eu, who had supplied 60 ships for the invasion. Rebuilding in stone, together with a chapel of St Mary, is said to have been ordered in 1070, and the church of St Mary within the walls later served a college of canons. The Counts of Eu held the lordship for most of the Norman period. When a later count chose his French lands over his English ones, Henry III gave the castle and honour to his queen's uncle Peter of Savoy in 1249, and from 1254 to 1262 they were held by the Lord Edward, the future Edward I of England.

The castle's military life was short. In 1216, with the future Louis VIII of France invading in support of the rebel barons, John of England ordered it slighted rather than let it fall to the French, and Henry III of England refortified it in 1220. The great storm of February 1287 brought down the soft sandstone cliff under part of the castle, and erosion carried more of it into the sea over the following centuries. Thomas Pelham bought the ruin in 1591, and it was farmed until it disappeared under undergrowth.

contentSections.title: Battle Abbey
paragraphs: The abbey on the battlefield was the great medieval foundation of the Hastings country. Its twelfth-century monks claimed that William had vowed before the fight to build a monastery if he won; more likely the foundation answered the penance that papal legates imposed on the invaders in 1070. Monks came from the Benedictine abbey of Marmoutier on the Loire, and the church, dedicated to the Holy Trinity, St Mary and St Martin, was built with its high altar where Harold was believed to have fallen, although the top of the ridge had to be levelled and built up to take it. It was finished around 1094, in the reign of William II of England, who gave the monks his father's sword and coronation robe.

The Conqueror's grant freed the abbey from the bishop of Chichester and gave its abbot rights over the lands around it. Abbot Walter de Luci defended that freedom against Bishop Hilary of Chichester before Henry II of England at Colchester in 1157, producing charters of William I and Henry I of England that the king accepted as genuine; many modern historians regard the Battle charters as forged at the abbey. Its monks also wrote the Chronicle of Battle Abbey, the source of the story of the Malfosse, a hidden ditch in which many men of both armies fell and were trampled.

A town grew at the abbey gate, where a settlement probably existed by 1110, and its parish church of St Mary was consecrated in 1115; the stonemasons John of Battle and Thomas of Battle, probably born there, later worked on royal building works under Edward I. The abbey church was remodelled in the late thirteenth century and the great gatehouse added in the fourteenth. Only seventeen monks remained when the abbey was surrendered in May 1538, and Henry VIII gave it to his Master of the Horse, Sir Anthony Browne, who pulled down the church and turned the abbot's lodging into a house. A plaque now marks the site of the high altar.

contentSections.title: The medieval town and the sea
paragraphs: Medieval Hastings was a narrow town in the valley below the castle, with its fishing boats drawn up on the shingle. The late Saxon port had lain further west, in the valley of the Priory Stream below the White Rock headland, but Danish attacks and floods in 1011 and 1014 are said to have driven its people east to the new borough. Around 1153 the geographer al-Idrisi, writing in Sicily, described Hastings as a large, flourishing and handsome town with markets, craftsmen and rich merchants.

The papal taxation survey of 1291 counted seven churches in the town. Two survive in the Old Town, All Saints at the foot of the East Hill and St Clement's, both largely rebuilt in the century after the French raids. Fish paid for them: in 1329 a priest was threatened with excommunication for failing to pay the bishop of Chichester the customary 2,000 herring, and boats still work from the beach below the old town.

contentSections.title: A head port of the Cinque Ports
paragraphs: Hastings was one of the five original Cinque Ports, with New Romney, Hythe, Dover and Sandwich. Their privileges probably began under Edward the Confessor, who gave south-eastern ports the profits of local justice in return for ships; a royal charter of 1155 obliged them to keep ships ready for the crown, and the first general charter of their liberties dates from 1260. Together they owed 57 ships for fifteen days of service a year, and in return were exempt from royal taxes and tallage and held their own courts, with rights over wrecks, felons and trade within their liberties.

Hastings often headed the list: Henry II's charters to Rye and Winchelsea in 1155 were addressed to the barons of Hastings and the Cinque Ports, probably because the ports were listed from west to east. Rye and Winchelsea joined by 1190 to help Hastings supply its share of ships and grew into Ancient Towns with the same standing as the head ports, while smaller places along the coast served as limbs. From the thirteenth century the ports sent members to Parliament. Winchelsea, rebuilt on a hill by Edward I after storms destroyed the old town in 1287 and 1288, became the busiest of Hastings' partners through its wine trade with Gascony.

contentSections.title: Storms, raids and decline
paragraphs: The storm of February 1287, which also choked New Romney's harbour and turned the Rother towards Rye, washed away much of Hastings' shore and part of its castle. The Hundred Years' War then brought French fleets to the Channel coast, and Hastings was raided and burned in 1339 and again in 1377, as Winchelsea was in the same decades. It never recovered as a port: the larger ships of the later Middle Ages could not use its beach, attempts to build a stone harbour under Elizabeth I were broken by storms, and in 1801 the town had only about 3,000 people.

contentSections.title: Hastings beyond Sussex
paragraphs: Hastings mattered far beyond its size. In 1066 it was the base from which William of Normandy fought the battle that opened the Norman Conquest of England, and the battle carried its name into every later history. Its castle anchored the lordship of eastern Sussex held by the Counts of Eu, a family with lands on both sides of the Channel, which tied the coast to Normandy for more than a century.

The abbey on the battlefield was a royal monument to the conquest whose monks shaped the memory of 1066 through their chronicle and their claims; the later Battle Abbey Roll of families said to have fought with William was padded with so many invented names that its surviving copies are now treated with caution. As a Cinque Port the town supplied ships and seamen to English kings through the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, until the sea it lived by took its harbour away.

sectionImages.caption: Norman workmen digging a castle mound 'at Hestenga ceastra' in the Bayeux Tapestry, embroidered probably in England in the 1070s.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown embroiderers, probably working for Odo, bishop of Bayeux
sectionImages.source: Bayeux Museum; image via Ulrich Harsch's website and Wikimedia Commons (public domain)
sectionImages.note: The inscription says that William ordered a castle to be dug at Hestenga ceastra. Because names ending in -ceaster usually mark Roman forts, and none is known at Hastings, some historians think the scene shows the fort the Normans built inside the Roman walls at Pevensey.

sectionImages.section: The castle and the Counts of Eu
sectionImages.caption: Hastings Castle on its cliff above the shore, a watercolour made by Samuel Hieronymus Grimm in 1784.
sectionImages.creator: Samuel Hieronymus Grimm
sectionImages.source: British Library, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain)
sectionImages.note: Drawn, as its inscription says, from the road on the west side of the priory ruins, when the castle site had been farmland for two centuries. The storm of 1287 and later erosion had already taken much of the castle into the sea, so the walls on the summit are only its landward remnant.

sectionImages.caption: The great gatehouse of Battle Abbey, founded on the field of 1066, in a colour photochrom print of about 1890.
sectionImages.creator: Detroit Publishing Company (photochrom print)
sectionImages.date: about 1890 (listed in the company's catalogue of 1905)

sectionImages.note: The gatehouse is the abbey's best-preserved medieval building and is usually dated to the fourteenth century; tree-ring study in 2016 also found fifteenth-century work in the abbey ranges. The colour was added in printing, and the wings on either side were altered after the abbey became a private house in 1538.
